Pavahārī Bābā
(‘the saint whose ड़ोओद् was air’)
------------------------------------------
It is the sages and saints—whether of the past or of the present—that have shaped the religio-cultured history of India over the last few millennia.
One such highly respected person who lived towards the end of the 19th century was Pavahārī Bābā—sometimes called Pāvanhārī Bābā also—the saint of Ghāzīpur near Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh. He was a great devotee of Lord राम.
It is said that he left home at the early age of fifteen or sixteen and started travelling as a religious mendicant. When he reached Badarīnāth, the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे in the हिमालयस्, he found a great saint who initiated him into the mysteries of योग.
After spending a long time in austerities under his guidance he came to Ghāzīpur and settled down there in a small cave-like structure. He is said to have been immersed in समाधि here for a long period of sixteen years!
When he opened his eyes, there was a huge crowd of people to see him and get his blessings. They arranged a grand festival in his honour and fed a large number of people on that occasion. The Bābā is said to have performed some miracles at that time.
An incident that is often quoted with regard to his greatness is how a thief that came to steal was converted by his goodness and loving concern.
Svāmi Vivekānanda had met him during his long sojourn as an itinerant monk.

Pavitrāropaṇa-vrata
------------------------------------------
It means investing the image of a deity with the पवित्र or the sacred cord. This ritual is supposed to set right all defects and mistakes committed in all the pūjās performed during that year. The putting on of the पवित्र in the case of several gods is done on different days. It may be made of gold, silver, copper, silk or even कुश or cotton thread. It must have knots, the maximum number being 100 and a minimum of 8.

pavitra
(‘the pure,’ ‘[what makes one ceremonially] pure’)
------------------------------------------
While performing any religious rite, a Hindu is expected to wear a ‘pavitra’. It is a ring-like loop made of दर्भ (Poa cynosuroides) grass. It may be prepared either with three or two or even one दर्भ leaf. It should be worn on the anāmika or the ring-finger, either of the right hand or on the ring-fingers of both the hands.
The following are the occasions on which the पवित्र is to be worn, to attain ceremonial fitness: जप (repetition of the divine name or mantras), होम (pouring oblations into a duly consecrated fire), दान (giving gifts), स्वाध्याय (study of the scriptures, especially the वेदस्) and तर्पण (giving oblations of water to the पितृस् or manes).
The word is also used to indicate the two pieces of दर्भ kept over आज्य (ghee) to purify it before होम, to the piece of cloth used by a saṁnyāsin to filter water while filling it into his कमण्डलु (water-pot) and even to the यज्ञोपवीत (the sacred thread).

Pavamānasūkta
(‘prayer concerning Pavamāna-सोम’)
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known सूक्त or prayer appearing in the Ṛgveda (9.1.1-10). Madhucchandā is the sage and Pavamāna-सोम is the deity. It is composed in the गायत्री metre.
This prayer is actually addressed to the सोम juice considered as a deity.
The word ‘pavamāna’ literally means ‘flowing’; hence Pavamāna-सोम is the deity of सोम juice which is flowing.
However the word ‘pavamāna,’ in course of time, came to be associated with or applied to वायु or the wind-god.
The Ṛgvedic prayer requests the deity to flow in torrents, to destroy the enemies (the demons), grant wealth and ड़ोओद् as also strength.
It also mentions that when इन्द्र, the king of gods, drinks this सोम juice, becomes exhilarated and fulfills all the desires of the supplicants like destroying their enemies and granting wealth.
Dharmaśāstra works often prescribe this सूक्त to be used as a मन्त्र for the purification of the bones of a dead person; to be repeated in śrāddha ceremonies; and as a purifier when sins have been committed.
